claim: Drosophila suzukii invaded the continental United States in 2008.
source: It invaded the continental United States in 2008 and is now found in at least 52 countries worldwide (Andreazza et al., 2017; Calabria et al., 2012; Dos Santos et al., 2017; Hauser, 2011; Ørsted et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Drosophila suzukii is now found in at least 52 countries worldwide.
source: It invaded the continental United States in 2008 and is now found in at least 52 countries worldwide (Andreazza et al., 2017; Calabria et al., 2012; Dos Santos et al., 2017; Hauser, 2011; Ørsted et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Most Drosophila species, including Drosophila melanogaster, prefer to lay eggs on fermenting fruits.
source: Most Drosophila species, including Drosophila melanogaster, prefer to lay eggs on fermenting fruits.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about Drosophila behavior.

claim: D. suzukii has an egg-laying preference for ripe, intact fruits.
source: By contrast, D. suzukii has an egg-laying preference for ripe, intact fruits (Cini et al., 2012; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and reference to figure data.

claim: D. suzukii females have an enlarged saw-like ovipositor that can pierce the skin of intact fruits and insert eggs underneath.
source: D. suzukii females have an enlarged saw-like ovipositor that can pierce the skin of intact fruits and insert eggs underneath (Poyet et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: D. melanogaster females select egg-laying sites by evaluating many cues, which inform them of nutrients, microbes, predators, and other flies.
source: D. melanogaster females select egg-laying sites by evaluating many cues, which inform them of nutrients, microbes, predators, and other flies (Ebrahim et al., 2015; Lin et al., 2015; Stensmyr et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Long-range localization of appropriate egg-laying sites relies mainly on olfaction and vision in D. melanogaster.
source: Multiple sensory modalities are used: long-range localization of appropriate sites relies mainly on olfaction and vision, whereas close-range decisions rely on contact-dependent gustatory and mechanosensory signals (Markow, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Close-range egg-laying decisions rely on contact-dependent gustatory and mechanosensory signals in D. melanogaster.
source: Multiple sensory modalities are used: long-range localization of appropriate sites relies mainly on olfaction and vision, whereas close-range decisions rely on contact-dependent gustatory and mechanosensory signals (Markow, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Changes in olfactory and mechanosensory responses contribute to the egg-laying shift in D. suzukii.
source: A pioneering study showed elegantly that changes in olfactory and mechanosensory responses contribute to the shift, but left open the possibility that other changes might contribute as well (Karageorgi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: D. suzukii's egg-laying preference has been found to correlate with the phosphorus content of fruits.
source: D. suzukii's egg-laying preference has been found to correlate with the phosphorus content of fruits (Olazcuaga et al., 2019), and the protein:carbohydrate ratio may be another cue (Silva-Soares et al., 2017; Young et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The protein:carbohydrate ratio may be a cue for D. suzukii's egg-laying preference.
source: D. suzukii's egg-laying preference has been found to correlate with the phosphorus content of fruits (Olazcuaga et al., 2019), and the protein:carbohydrate ratio may be another cue (Silva-Soares et al., 2017; Young et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature and involves speculative reasoning about potential cues.

claim: A recent study found a difference between D. suzukii and D. melanogaster in egg-laying preference for high sucrose concentrations.
source: A recent study found a difference between D. suzukii and D. melanogaster in egg-laying preference for high sucrose concentrations (Durkin et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: D. suzukii and D. melanogaster sense bitter compounds differently.
source: An extensive behavioral, electrophysiological, and molecular analysis of taste organs recently showed that D. suzukii and D. melanogaster sense bitter compounds differently (Dweck et al., 2021), inviting a comparable comparison of the sensation of other salient taste cues.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: D. melanogaster without olfactory organs showed a robust preference for overripe strawberry purée over ripe strawberry purée.
source: Deprived of these other cues, D. melanogaster showed a robust preference for the overripe purée, while D. suzukii did not (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: D. suzukii without olfactory organs did not show a preference for overripe strawberry purée over ripe strawberry purée.
source: Deprived of these other cues, D. melanogaster showed a robust preference for the overripe purée, while D. suzukii did not (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Taste contributes to the difference in egg-laying preference between D. melanogaster and D. suzukii.
source: The simplest interpretation of this result is that taste contributes to the difference in egg-laying preference between the two species.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing differences in egg-laying preferences when olfactory, visual, and mechanosensory cues are minimized.

claim: D. melanogaster octuple mutant flies lacking eight sugar receptor genes showed a lower preference for overripe strawberry purée than control flies.
source: After their olfactory organs had been removed, these mutant flies showed a lower preference for overripe strawberry purée than control flies whose olfactory organs had also been removed (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Sugar sensation contributes to the preference of D. melanogaster for overripe fruit purée.
source: These results suggest that sugar sensation contributes to the preference of D. melanogaster for overripe fruit purée.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results with sugar receptor mutants.

claim: D. suzukii showed a weaker egg-laying preference than D. melanogaster for substrates containing 100 mM sucrose versus 0 mM sucrose.
source: Both D. suzukii and D. melanogaster preferred the medium with 100 mM sucrose to that with no sucrose, but the preference of D. suzukii was weaker than that of D. melanogaster (Figure 2B), consistent with a recent study that used higher concentrations (Durkin et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and a citation to published literature.

claim: D. melanogaster showed a strong preference for 100 mM sucrose over 10 mM sucrose, but D. suzukii showed little if any preference.
source: When choosing between 100 mM and 10 mM sucrose, D. melanogaster again showed a strong preference for the higher concentration, but D. suzukii showed little if any preference.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from egg-laying preference assays.

claim: D. suzukii exhibited a weaker preference than D. melanogaster when choosing between 100 mM and 30 mM sucrose or between 100 mM and 60 mM sucrose.
source: And when choosing between 100 mM and 30 mM or between 100 mM and 60 mM sucrose, D. suzukii again exhibited a weaker preference than D. melanogaster.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from egg-laying preference assays.

claim: Fructose elicited weaker egg-laying preferences from D. suzukii than D. melanogaster in each of four preference tests.
source: Fructose also elicited weaker preferences from D. suzukii than D. melanogaster, in each of the four preference tests (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: D. suzukii showed no preference for higher fructose concentrations in three out of four tests, while D. melanogaster preferred the higher concentration.
source: Whereas D. melanogaster preferred the higher concentration of fructose in the other three tests, D. suzukii showed no preference.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from egg-laying preference assays.

claim: In every glucose comparison, D. suzukii showed a weaker preference for the higher sugar concentration than D. melanogaster.
source: Glucose showed similar results: in every comparison, D. suzukii showed a weaker preference for the higher sugar concentration than D. melanogaster (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Flies of both species showed strong preferences for 100 mM sucrose over 100 mM sorbitol.
source: In fact, flies of both species showed strong preferences to 100 mM sucrose (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The preferences of flies for 100 mM sucrose over 100 mM sorbitol were the same as those between 100 mM sucrose and plain medium.
source: Moreover, the preferences were the same as those between 100 mM sucrose and plain medium, as if they are insensitive to the osmolarity of sorbitol.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing different conditions.

claim: D. suzukii and D. melanogaster differ in their response to sweetness.
source: The simplest interpretation of these results is that D. suzukii and D. melanogaster differ in their response to sweetness.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing differential responses to sugars versus sorbitol.

claim: D. suzukii showed a weaker egg-laying preference for sweeter substrates than D. melanogaster.
source: In conclusion, D. suzukii showed a weaker egg-laying preference for sweeter substrates than D. melanogaster.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental results.

claim: There are 31 taste sensilla in the labellum of D. melanogaster: 11 small (S) sensilla, 9 large (L) sensilla, and 11 intermediate (I) sensilla.
source: There are 31 taste sensilla in the labellum, the primary taste organ of the D. melanogaster head: 11 small (S) sensilla, 9 large (L) sensilla, and 11 intermediate (I) sensilla (Weiss et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The sensillum repertoire of D. suzukii is similar in spatial organization to D. melanogaster but has lost two S sensilla and two I sensilla.
source: The sensillum repertoire of D. suzukii is similar in its spatial organization but has lost two S sensilla and two I sensilla (Figure 3A; Dweck et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by figure data and a citation to published literature.

claim: Sucrose elicited responses from all 11 of the S sensilla in D. melanogaster, but only 3 of the S sensilla in D. suzukii.
source: Sucrose elicited responses from all 11 of the S sensilla in D. melanogaster, but only 3 of the S sensilla in D. suzukii (Figure 3B top traces, Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Fructose evoked responses of more than 10 spikes/s from all 9 of the L sensilla in D. melanogaster, but not from any of their D. suzukii counterparts.
source: Fructose evoked responses of more than 10 spikes/s from all 9 of the L sensilla in D. melanogaster, but not from any of their D. suzukii counterparts (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Glucose responses were comparable in the two species.
source: Glucose responses were comparable in the two species (Figure 3I–K).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3I-K.

claim: The number and spatial organization of taste sensilla on the three distal tarsal segments of the D. suzukii female foreleg are stereotyped and similar to those in D. melanogaster.
source: We found that the number and spatial organization of taste sensilla on the three distal tarsal segments of the D. suzukii female foreleg are stereotyped and similar to those in D. melanogaster (Figure 3L).
evidence: The claim is supported by observational data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Five D. suzukii female foreleg sensilla responded to sucrose, fructose, and glucose at 100 mM concentrations.
source: When tested with sucrose, fructose, and glucose at 100 mM concentrations, five D. suzukii female foreleg sensilla responded; other sensilla did not (Figure 3M–O).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3M-O.

claim: The pattern of sugar responses in D. suzukii female foreleg sensilla was the same as that observed in D. melanogaster.
source: This pattern of responses was the same as that observed in D. melanogaster (Ling et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with published literature.

claim: The dose-response relationships for sucrose in the L8 sensillum were comparable between D. suzukii and D. melanogaster, although not identical.
source: We tested the labellum sensillum L8 and the leg sensillum f5s of both species at a series of sucrose concentrations and found that the dose-response relationships were comparable, although not identical; for example, the responses of f5s were lower in D. suzukii at the higher concentrations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B, D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The responses of f5s sensillum were lower in D. suzukii at higher sucrose concentrations.
source: We tested the labellum sensillum L8 and the leg sensillum f5s of both species at a series of sucrose concentrations and found that the dose-response relationships were comparable, although not identical; for example, the responses of f5s were lower in D. suzukii at the higher concentrations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B, D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: L8 and f5s sensilla in both species give distinguishable physiological responses to 1 mM sucrose vs. 10 mM sucrose and to 10 mM sucrose vs. 60 mM sucrose.
source: These sensilla, in both species, give distinguishable physiological responses to 1 mM sucrose vs. 10 mM sucrose and to 10 mM sucrose vs. 60 mM sucrose (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and F.

claim: Both species could distinguish behaviorally between 1 mM and 10 mM sucrose and between 10 mM and 60 mM sucrose.
source: Likewise, both species could also distinguish between these concentrations behaviorally (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: Flies of neither species distinguished behaviorally between 60 mM and 100 mM sucrose.
source: By contrast, flies of neither species distinguished behaviorally between 60 mM and 100 mM sucrose, and physiologically, the sensilla we examined did not distinguish between these concentrations in three of four cases (L8 of D. suzukii and f5s of both species; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral and physiological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A major subset of S sensilla have lost response to sucrose in D. suzukii.
source: A major subset of S sensilla have lost response to sucrose in D. suzukii, and L sensilla have lost response to fructose.
evidence: The claim is a summary of electrophysiological findings.

claim: L sensilla have lost response to fructose in D. suzukii.
source: A major subset of S sensilla have lost response to sucrose in D. suzukii, and L sensilla have lost response to fructose.
evidence: The claim is a summary of electrophysiological findings.

claim: These losses in sugar responses could contribute to the weaker egg-laying preference of D. suzukii for sweeter substrates.
source: These losses could contribute to the weaker egg-laying preference of D. suzukii for sweeter substrates.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between physiological losses and behavioral differences.

claim: Expression of 13 Gustatory receptor (Gr) genes was detected in the leg of D. melanogaster.
source: By focusing our analysis on leg segments containing taste sensilla, we were able to detect the expression of 13 Gustatory receptor (Gr) genes in the leg of D. melanogaster (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Nine Gr genes previously identified as sugar receptor genes (Gr5a, Gr43a, Gr61a, and Gr64a-f) were detected in the leg of D. melanogaster.
source: These included the nine Gr genes previously identified as sugar receptor genes (Gr5a, Gr43a, Gr61a, and Gr64a-f) (Supplementary file 1), most of which have previously been found to be expressed in legs via GAL4 driver expression (Ling et al., 2014; Thoma et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data and citations to published literature.

claim: 13 Ionotropic receptors (IRs) were detected in the leg of D. melanogaster.
source: Also detected in the leg of D. melanogaster were 13 Ionotropic receptors (IRs), many of which have been detected in legs via GAL4 expression (Koh et al., 2014; Sánchez-Alcañiz et al., 2018), and 30 Odorant binding proteins (Obps) including several previously reported in the leg (Galindo and Smith, 2001; Jeong et al., 2013; Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data and citations to published literature.

claim: 30 Odorant binding proteins (Obps) were detected in the leg of D. melanogaster.
source: Also detected in the leg of D. melanogaster were 13 Ionotropic receptors (IRs), many of which have been detected in legs via GAL4 expression (Koh et al., 2014; Sánchez-Alcañiz et al., 2018), and 30 Odorant binding proteins (Obps) including several previously reported in the leg (Galindo and Smith, 2001; Jeong et al., 2013; Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data and citations to published literature.

claim: Principal components analysis showed clear clustering of transcriptomes by organ and by species.
source: A principal components analysis (PCA) showed clear clustering of transcriptomes by organ and by species (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Expression of three sugar receptor genes (Gr64a, Gr64d, and Gr64e) was reduced in D. suzukii legs with an adjusted p-value<0.05.
source: Among the nine sugar receptor genes, expression of three (Gr64a, Gr64d, and Gr64e) was reduced in D. suzukii with an adjusted p-value<0.05 (Figure 4B and C, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 4B and C and Supplementary file 3.

claim: None of the sugar Grs showed a higher level of expression in D. suzukii legs than D. melanogaster legs.
source: None of the sugar Grs showed a higher level of expression in D. suzukii than D. melanogaster.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis.

claim: Gr64d was not detected at all in D. suzukii legs (TPM = 0).
source: Gr64d was not detected at all in D. suzukii (TPM (transcripts per million) = 0, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The level of Gr64a in D. suzukii legs was reduced to 41% of that in D. melanogaster legs (adjusted p-value<0.0001).
source: The level of Gr64a was reduced to 41% of that in D. melanogaster (adjusted p-value<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis.

claim: RT-qPCR confirmed the reduced expression level of Gr64a, Gr64d, and Gr64e in D. suzukii legs.
source: To verify the differential expression of the three sugar Grs that were found by RNAseq to be expressed at lower levels in the legs of D. suzukii, we performed RT-quantitative PCR (qPCR). The reduced expression level in D. suzukii was confirmed in all cases (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Expression of eight sugar Grs (Gr5a, Gr61a, and Gr64a-f) was detected in the labellum transcriptome of each species.
source: In the labellum transcriptome of each species, expression of eight sugar Grs was detected (Gr5a, Gr61a, and Gr64a-f), consistent with several previous studies (Dahanukar et al., 2001; Dahanukar et al., 2007; Jiao et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data and citations to published literature.

claim: Expression of seven sugar Grs (Gr5a, Gr61a, Gr64a, Gr64b, Gr64d, Gr64e, and Gr64f) was reduced in D. suzukii labellum with an adjusted p-value<0.05.
source: Among these Grs, expression of seven (Gr5a, Gr61a, Gr64a, Gr64b, Gr64d, Gr64e, and Gr64f) was reduced in D. suzukii with an adjusted p-value<0.05; levels of the other two Grs did not differ significantly (Figure 4E and F, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 4E and F and Supplementary file 4.

claim: The expression of Gr64d in D. suzukii labellum was reduced to only 15% of its level in D. melanogaster labellum (adjusted p-value<0.001).
source: The expression of Gr64d was reduced in D. suzukii to only 15% of its level in D. melanogaster (adjusted p-value<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis.

claim: RT-qPCR confirmed the reduced expression in D. suzukii labellum for Gr5a, Gr61a, Gr64a, Gr64d, and Gr64e.
source: The reduced expression in D. suzukii was confirmed by RT-qPCR for Gr5a, Gr61a, Gr64a, Gr64d, and Gr64e (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Gr5a has been identified as a receptor for trehalose.
source: One of the Gr genes expressed at lower levels in the D. suzukii labellum than in the D. melanogaster labellum, according to both RNAseq and RT-qPCR results, was Gr5a, which has been identified as a receptor for trehalose (Dahanukar et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: D. suzukii showed a weaker egg-laying preference for 100 mM trehalose versus plain medium than D. melanogaster.
source: When presented with a choice between 100 mM trehalose and plain medium, D. suzukii showed a weaker egg-laying preference for trehalose than D. melanogaster (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Lower levels of Gr expression may contribute to the weaker egg-laying preference of D. suzukii for sweeter substrates.
source: These results suggest that lower levels of Gr expression may contribute to the weaker egg-laying preference of D. suzukii for sweeter substrates.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between reduced Gr expression and weaker behavioral preferences.

claim: D. suzukii laid fewer eggs than D. melanogaster in the trehalose experiment.
source: We noted that in this experiment with trehalose, D. suzukii laid fewer eggs than D. melanogaster (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Trehalose is a less potent egg-laying stimulus for D. suzukii than D. melanogaster.
source: This finding suggests that trehalose is a less potent egg-laying stimulus for D. suzukii than D. melanogaster, which could also result at least in part from lower expression of Gr5a.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that D. suzukii laid fewer eggs in the presence of trehalose.

claim: Trehalose is a sugar present in yeast.
source: Interestingly, trehalose is a sugar present in yeast (Jules et al., 2008; Jules et al., 2004), which populate overripe fruits that are oviposition sites for D. melanogaster but not D. suzukii.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Yeast populate overripe fruits that are oviposition sites for D. melanogaster but not D. suzukii.
source: Interestingly, trehalose is a sugar present in yeast (Jules et al., 2008; Jules et al., 2004), which populate overripe fruits that are oviposition sites for D. melanogaster but not D. suzukii.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the oviposition preferences of the two species.

claim: Previous studies have found a difference between D. suzukii and D. melanogaster in their egg-laying preference for stiff substrates.
source: Previous studies have found a difference between D. suzukii and D. melanogaster in their egg-laying preference for stiff substrates (Durkin et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2020; Karageorgi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: D. suzukii laid the fewest eggs on the softest substrate (0.1% agarose), whereas D. melanogaster laid the fewest eggs on the hardest substrate (2% agarose).
source: We found that D. suzukii laid the fewest eggs on the softest substrate, whereas D. melanogaster laid the fewest eggs on the hardest substrate (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: D. melanogaster preferred the softer substrate (0.25% agarose), while D. suzukii preferred the harder substrate (1.5% agarose) in a two-choice assay.
source: We then directly compared the preferences of the two species in a two-choice assay. D. melanogaster preferred the softer substrate, while D. suzukii preferred the harder substrate (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Expression of nine mechanosensory channel genes (iav, nompC, pain, Piezo, ppk, ppk26, Tmc, rpk, and tmem63) was found in both legs and labellum.
source: Taking advantage of the transcriptomes of the legs and the labellum—organs that make direct physical contact with egg-laying sites—we found expression of nine mechanosensory channels genes (iav, nompC, pain, Piezo, ppk, ppk26, Tmc, rpk, and tmem63; ≥1 TPM, Supplementary file 2), all of which were expressed in both legs and labellum.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: In the legs, six mechanosensory genes (iav, nompC, pain, ppk26, Tmc, and tmem63) were expressed at higher levels in D. suzukii (adjusted p-value<0.05).
source: In the legs, six of these mechanosensory genes (iav, nompC, pain, ppk26, Tmc, and tmem63) were expressed at higher levels in D. suzukii (Figure 6C, adjusted p-value<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Leg expression of nompC was approximately fourfold higher in D. suzukii (adjusted p-value<0.0001).
source: Particularly striking was the ~fourfold higher expression of nompC (adjusted p-value<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis.

claim: In the labellum, levels of four mechanosensory genes (nompC, pain, Piezo, and tmem63) were higher in D. suzukii (adjusted p-value<0.05).
source: In the labellum, levels of four of these mechanosensory genes (nompC, pain, Piezo, and tmem63) were again higher in D. suzukii (Figure 6D, adjusted p-value<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Labellar expression of nompC was more than sevenfold higher in D. suzukii than in D. melanogaster (adjusted p-value<0.0001).
source: Remarkably, labellar expression of nompC was more than sevenfold higher than that of D. melanogaster (adjusted p-value<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data analysis.

claim: None of the mechanosensory genes were expressed at lower levels in D. suzukii than in D. melanogaster, in either the legs or labellum.
source: None of the mechanosensory genes were expressed at lower levels in D. suzukii than in D. melanogaster, in either the legs or labellum (Supplementary files 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq data in Supplementary files 3 and 4.

claim: RT-qPCR analysis revealed higher levels of nompC in D. suzukii than D. melanogaster, in both the legs and labella.
source: Consistent with these RNAseq results, RT-qPCR analysis revealed higher levels of nompC in D. suzukii than D. melanogaster, in both the legs and labella (Figure 6E and F); leg RNA was again prepared from dissected tibia and tarsi of female forelegs.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: RT-qPCR analysis confirmed higher expression levels of Tmc in the legs and Piezo in the labellum of D. suzukii.
source: RT-qPCR analysis also confirmed higher expression levels of Tmc in the legs and Piezo in the labellum.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data analysis.

claim: D. suzukii has a lower preference for sweet and lower levels of sugar receptors.
source: In summary, whereas D. suzukii has a lower preference for sweet and lower levels of sugar receptors, it has a higher preference for stiff substrates and higher levels of certain mechanosensory channels in its legs and labellum.
evidence: The claim is a summary of multiple experimental findings.

claim: D. suzukii has a higher preference for stiff substrates and higher levels of certain mechanosensory channels in its legs and labellum.
source: In summary, whereas D. suzukii has a lower preference for sweet and lower levels of sugar receptors, it has a higher preference for stiff substrates and higher levels of certain mechanosensory channels in its legs and labellum.
evidence: The claim is a summary of multiple experimental findings.

claim: When both substrates contained 100 mM sucrose, D. melanogaster showed no preference for the softer substrate (0.5% vs. 1% agarose).
source: When both substrates contained 100 mM sucrose, D. melanogaster showed no preference for the softer substrate (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: When the sucrose concentration in both substrates was reduced to 30 mM, D. melanogaster showed a preference for the softer substrate (p<0.01).
source: When the sucrose concentration in both substrates was reduced to 30 mM, a preference emerged (p<0.01); when the sucrose concentration was further reduced to 10 mM, the preference was again clear (p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data with statistical analysis.

claim: When the sucrose concentration was reduced to 10 mM, D. melanogaster showed a clear preference for the softer substrate (p<0.001).
source: When the sucrose concentration in both substrates was reduced to 30 mM, a preference emerged (p<0.01); when the sucrose concentration was further reduced to 10 mM, the preference was again clear (p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data with statistical analysis.

claim: High sweetness can mask the preference for softness in D. melanogaster.
source: These results support the notion that high sweetness can mask the preference for softness.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental results showing that preference for softness emerges at lower sugar concentrations.

claim: D. suzukii showed no preference for softer substrate in the presence of 100 mM sucrose.

claim: The dramatic differences between the two species in sugar preferences examined on hard substrates (1% agarose) were not observed on softer substrates (0.5% agarose).
source: Specifically, we wondered if the dramatic differences between the two species in sugar preferences examined on hard substrates (1% agarose; Figure 2B, shown again for convenience as Figure 7B) would also be observed on softer substrates (0.5% agarose). They were not, in that the responses of the two species were indistinguishable in all but one case (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: In D. melanogaster, the preference for the sweeter substrate (100 mM vs. 30 mM sucrose at 1% agarose) vanished when the sweeter substrate was also harder.
source: We then extended these results by choosing the most dramatic difference between the two species, the preference for 100 mM sucrose vs. 30 mM sucrose at 1% agarose, and asking how this preference changed when the sweeter substrate was also harder. In the case of D. melanogaster, the preference for the sweeter substrate vanished (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In D. suzukii, a preference for the sweeter substrate emerged when the sweeter substrate was also harder.

evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data from the experiment described.
